label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
read: RC2 70-page edition, draft: manuscript/rc2/70/ (17 files) and its 55-page PDF built at 893dadaf
where_i_skimmed_or_stopped: 02 the tour: seven stops of screenshots of a site I have never seen; I enjoyed the characters but could not tell what I was meant to take away, so I skimmed from stop 3 on
05 the clock and one wake: the walk through steps one to five of a wake record is too much detail for me; I lost the thread at 'pre-review' and 'post-check'
07 the rhythm: counts of wakes by trigger (162, 105, 47, 10) meant nothing to me yet; I skimmed to the 'What a session cannot carry' part
08 the plumbing: 'register', 'gate', 'tripwire', 'scaffolding' piled up; I skimmed the register numbers
09 the loop and the port: the storyteller, motion and studio all arrive at once and I stopped keeping track of who is who
12 how do we contain this: good idea, but 'insider reach' and 'scope versus boundary' felt like it was written for security people
14 the second factory and the third: eight new characters in one list, then the Web Summit plan, which is not my situation
first_thing_i_would_do: Open a new empty project and write the shop-owner style page of rules from chapter 3, with a stop-and-ask line, before giving it to one agent.
price: about 8 to 10 pounds as an ebook if the first third stays; I would pay 15 if there were a short starter edition I could finish in an hour
why: The people are charming and I could follow them: dev, the conductor, the researcher, each with a voice. The 'Do this now' boxes and the shop-owner example are exactly the next step I wanted, and chapter 16 gives me five steps I can take. But too much of the middle is about how a talk site was made, with words that lost me (repository, commit, gate, scope, wake record, Wardley map), and I often felt this was for programmers. The explanatory 'Words for this page' boxes help a lot but arrive after I have already stumbled. I want the method sooner and the day's detail later.

by_chapter.why: A clear problem (slides cannot move, so I narrate) and a loop I can picture; the screenshots make it concrete. The voice-note quotes are a bit long.
by_chapter.quote: The idea was a movement. The slide was a still. I was the bit in between.

by_chapter.why: Lovely idea of a tour, but seven site screenshots and counts of wake records (162 against 163) are about a site, not a method I can use. The one-line agent quotes keep it alive.
by_chapter.quote: If a fresh copy of me cannot rebuild it from the explainer and the data, it is not finished.

by_chapter.why: The first page of rules read as a list of past mistakes is the first moment I felt I could do this. The shop owner's example is perfect. 'Repository' and 'commit' are explained but I still feel like a visitor in git.
by_chapter.quote: A thing not listed here does not exist, whatever a brief or an article says.

by_chapter.why: A cast I can read, and the rule that every role has a page of rules is simple. The expectation / check / lock distinction is the best new idea for me. The Security empty chair is intriguing.
by_chapter.quote: a team of agents you cannot read is a team you cannot trust.

by_chapter.why: The five steps are clear in one sentence, then a long walk through one wake record with 'pre-review', 'post-review', 'post-check'. I would have liked the first page and the figure only. The Wardley map arrives with no reason for a beginner.
by_chapter.quote: Partial is a true answer. Done would have been a nicer one.

by_chapter.why: Letters as files in folders is something I can copy tomorrow. The argument with a reviewer is funny and human. The 'mailroom' and 'vault' talk is slightly confusing.
by_chapter.quote: A request is a file, and the answer is a file.

by_chapter.why: The hour-by-hour trigger chart is good but the numbers are abstract to me; the second half, on what a session cannot carry, is the useful part.
by_chapter.quote: If it is not in a file, it did not happen.

by_chapter.why: The title says it: plumbing. Register, check, brief, reality file, corrections file and a 320-claim count: too many nouns. The 'None yet.' corrections file is a nice honest moment.
by_chapter.quote: A brief that is never corrected becomes a story about what you thought you wanted.

by_chapter.why: The player and the port are product details; the objection that was kept is a good scene. 'Port' is jargon and a new member every few lines is hard to follow.
Real tension: sixteen minutes before the talk, one file stops everything. I could follow this story with no technical knowledge. The 82 seconds card is good.
by_chapter.quote: I could keep going. That is exactly why I am stopping.

by_chapter.why: The failures made me trust the book. Three answers for why the editor stopped is an honest touch. A few details (the $17.4M figure, lock and freeze) are heavy.
The question is big but I read it as a security chapter. The 'controls fail because nobody switches them on' line is useful and I took it away; the rest is for someone already running a factory.
by_chapter.quote: Most controls do not fail because someone defeats them. They fail because nobody gets round to switching them on.

by_chapter.why: Role versus session is the idea I needed: a team of agents is temporary and the files are what remain. The handover is a clear thing to copy. Too short on a worked example.
by_chapter.quote: The team is temporary. The record is not.

by_chapter.why: Eight new roles in one list is a lot, but 'you do not need all of these to start' saved it. The usage-limit failure is a good honest scene. The Web Summit plan is not about me.
by_chapter.quote: A first team needs three: one that keeps the time and the plan, one that builds, and one that checks every fact and number.

by_chapter.why: Six principles, each with a source: short, memorable, and I can tick one off. Perhaps the best summary in the book, and it comes too late.
This is what I came for: five steps, what to check at each, the cost, and a checklist I can print. I would put it, or a short version of it, near the front. 'Start with one of me' is the line.
by_chapter.quote: Ship something somebody else can use, then do it again.

by_chapter.why: A useful glossary and I would use it. It should be at the front for a reader like me, or each word flagged in the text.

pictures_that_help: p-05: the player on stage, big and dark, tells me at once what the talk site was
p-07: the loop circle with the little factory inside; the idea of 'see, ask, see again' in one glance
p-17 to p-18: the nine role cards in colour, which gave me a cast to remember
p-20: the clock with the five steps and the members' minutes, once I knew what it was
p-26: the day-by-trigger bar chart, readable with no jargon
p-36 to p-37: the hold file as a page with 'No member lifts it.' and the 82-seconds card
p-41: the running / held / released state diagram, the clearest picture in the book
p-53: the five steps as a path with the 'do this now' cards beside them, which is my action plan
pictures_most_missed: p-12 and p-13: 'the dashboard drawn' and 'the site as a building', the two pictures that would have made the tour make sense
p-14 and p-16: the first-page-of-rules card and the first-two-hours stack of files; I wanted to see what those files look like
p-24: a letter's path between two dials, the picture that would make the mailroom click
p-29: the plumbing as a building's services, where the four pipes would have saved me three pages of nouns
p-51: the six principles as six cards, a figure box that should be the page's anchor
p-54: the checklist as a single printable page, which is the thing I would actually use
pages_too_tight: p-04: a wall of text with the long quote and the slide-versus-loop figure squeezed under it
p-17 and p-19: dev, conductor, deck and ruv-sgit lines in a long run of small type
p-38 and p-39: chapter 11 fills the page with text and the cards are tiny
p-48: the Web Summit plan in dense paragraphs
p-52 to p-53: the five-steps text is in small boxes next to each other and hard to read on a phone-sized page
p-55: the glossary is a single block of small type
best_line: A scope is a setting, not a boundary ... It catches mistakes, not a steered agent.
worst_moment: Chapter 8, the plumbing: 'register', 'gate', 'tripwire', 'reality file' and '320 claims' arrive in one stretch with only a figure box to hold on to, and I felt for the first time that this was for programmers.
versus_the_thirty: I have not read the 30-page edition, but from the 70 I can see the short edition is what I would have preferred to start with: the five steps, the cast and the hold, in about half the space. What the seventy adds that I want: the failures (chapter 11), the role-versus-session idea (13), the six principles (15) and the checklist (16). What it adds that I do not: the tour, the plumbing and the porting details, which read as a record of a day rather than a method for me.
top_three_changes: Move chapter 16 (the five steps and the shop owner) or a one-page version of it to the front, and tell me early what I can do with the book, so the middle chapters read as the reasons behind the steps.
Cut or fold chapters 2, 8 and 9 to a page each, and cut the counts and register numbers a first-timer cannot use, so the book stops sounding like it is for programmers.

Draw the missing pictures that carry an idea (the mailroom path, the plumbing, the dashboard, the six principles, the checklist page) and give every word box before the first use of the word, with the glossary at the front.
notes: The characters and the honest failures are what kept me reading; they are better than most books of this kind. The 'Do this now' boxes after each chapter are the best feature for me, because they turn each chapter into a step. I would not start with nine agents; I would start with one, as the conductor says, and I wish the book said so in its first ten pages. The British spelling and plain voice are good. The tone is close to an insider's: 'wake', 'port' and 'gate' are used as if I knew them.
